newsitem.title: MEXICO: Business leaders in Mexico praise NAFTA - AmCham.
newsitem.headline: Business leaders in Mexico praise NAFTA - AmCham.

text.p: Business leaders in Mexico believe the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) has led to greater coordination between Mexican, Canadian and U.S. firms, a recent American Chamber of Commerce report said.

Since NAFTA took effect on Jan. 1, 1994, 53.3 percent of Mexican respondents in the chamber's poll said they started some sort of "new formal relationship" with a U.S. company and 16 percent forged business ties with a Canadian company.

The number of respondents exporting to the United States rose to 42 percent in 1996 from 27 percent in 1993. Exporters in the survey rose to 76.7 percent in 1996 compared to 62 percent three years before.
"The benefit most often mentioned by survey respondents was the reduction of tariffs and duties and therefore, the reduction of costs," the American Chamber, known as the AmCham, wrote in the report.
According to the survey, some of the issues that impede trade were: backlogs at Mexican and U.S. customs, confusing labelling rules and other non-tariff barriers.
The AmCham said NAFTA has also promoted better environmental standards and improved work safety guidelines.

"Despite the gloomy forecasts made by critics of NAFTA, environmental and safety standards have actually increased under NAFTA," AmCham president and president of Citibank de Mexico Julio de Quesada said in the report.
The survey polled 227 companies, or 20.6 percent of chamber members. Its results were to be used in a formal U.S. government review of NAFTA on Tuesday.
